column1: # Purpose: supplemental defensive context for SUID and SGID findings.
#   documents Unix binaries that are commonly shipped with elevated privilege
#   and are known to be usable in unintended ways. This file does NOT reproduce
#   that project's content. It is an independent, deliberately small selection
#   with original one-sentence explanations written for this tool.
#   * This list is NOT exhaustive and is not a mirror of GTFOBins.
#   * It intentionally omits anything whose relevance depends on embedded
#     firmware, appliance vendor builds or historical vulnerabilities.
#   * Absence from this list is NOT evidence that a binary is safe.
#   * A match is contextual risk information only. It does not indicate that a
#     vulnerability was exploited, that a host is compromised, or that the
#   name     exact binary basename, no path separators, case sensitive
#   category one of: shell, interpreter, editor, archive, filesystem,
#   summary  one concise original sentence, no tabs or newlines
# Blank lines and lines beginning with '#' are ignored.
#   * Add an entry only when the binary is plausibly present on a general-purpose
#     Linux host and its presence with SUID/SGID is worth an analyst's time.
#   * Keep the summary defensive and descriptive. Never add usage instructions,
#   * Preserve the tab-separated shape; the loader rejects malformed lines.
#   * Names must be unique; the loader rejects duplicates.
# Source of the concept: GTFOBins, MIT licence, by the GTFOBins contributors.

column3: POSIX shell interpreter. Distributions never ship one with SUID or SGID set; if one does, any local user can run a full privileged shell.
GNU shell interpreter. Carries the same risk as any privileged interactive shell.
Minimal POSIX shell used as /bin/sh on Debian-derived systems.
Z shell interpreter. A privileged copy grants an interactive session with the owner's identity.
Korn shell interpreter. An interactive shell should never carry elevated privilege.
C shell interpreter.
Enhanced C shell interpreter.
Coreutils environment runner. It executes another program in a chosen environment, so a privileged copy lends its identity to arbitrary programs.
Pattern-scanning interpreter that evaluates a program supplied in its arguments or input.
GNU awk interpreter.
Lightweight awk interpreter used as the default awk on some distributions.
The One True Awk interpreter.
Interpreted language that executes program text taken from arguments, files or standard input.
Interpreted language interpreter.
Python 2 interpreter.

Interpreted language interpreter.
PHP language interpreter, also usable as a command line processor.
Lua interpreter; evaluates chunks of code supplied at run time.
Tcl interpreter, commonly embedded in network appliances.
Tcl/Tk windowing shell.
Automates interactive programs and is frequently shipped privileged in embedded devices.
Text editor. An editor started by a user on a privileged file opens a shell as that user.
Vi Improved, a common interactive editor.
Neovim editor.
Vi started in read-only mode.
Line editor derived from vi.
Classic line editor that accepts commands from standard input.
Extensible editor that can run arbitrary shell commands.

Stream editor that transforms its input using an expression given on the command line.
Archive utility that extracts and writes files, including ones with elevated ownership.

Recursive file walker that evaluates an expression supplied on the command line.

Synchronisation utility that writes files and can preserve attributes.
Creates hard and symbolic links.

Unmounts filesystems.
Command line downloader that retrieves arbitrary remote content to disk.
Command line transfer tool that can write arbitrary remote content to disk.

Netcat successor from the Nmap project.
Traditional netcat implementation.
Multipurpose relay that moves data between arbitrary endpoints.
File transfer client.
